newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Absa Hong Kong unit targets Asian investors.
newsitem.headline: Absa Hong Kong unit targets Asian investors.

text.p: Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Ltd (Absa) said on Tuesday that its Hong Kong-based unit Absa Asia Ltd has launched a property financing scheme for Asian investors aiming to puy property in South Africa.
Absa, South Africa's largest banking group with assets of more than $24 billion, said it was the first bank to offer South African property financing in this way.
It added in a statement that it had ready received a number of enquiries from interested parties.
"We expect enquires from commercial and industrial property investors as well as individuals seeking residential properties," said Ken Hughes, Absa Asia business development general manager.

The scheme will be available to qualifying non-resident buyers in U.S. dollars or Hong Kong dollars against legal mortgages on South African property for up to 70 percent of the property's value. Repayments will be over five years.

"If 100 percent of the purchase price is remitted from outside South Africa in foreign currency, then a non-resident foreign company like Absa Asia can take a mortgage on the property and provide an offshore loan," Hughes said.
Since it emerged from decades of white-minority rule South Africa has succeeded in attracting a wealth of business interest from Asian countries, especially Malaysia.

Recent figures show Malaysian firms invested 1.8 billion rand in South Africa between April 1994 and May 1996 and in August, 1996, the country's state-owned oil group Petronas Bhd poured 1.9 billion rand into buying a 30 percent stake of Engen Ltd.
However, relations with another important Asian trading partner, Taiwan, suffered a blow recently when South Africa ditched the country in favour of establishing diplomatic ties with mainland China.
Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province and refuses to establish formal ties with countries that recognise Taipei's sovereignty.
On January 19 Taiwan warned its businessmen South Africa now posed a potential investment risk.

Taipei would "adjust" its economic policies toward South Africa and investment activities originally aimed at cementing ties would be reconsidered, Cho Shih-chao, a deputy director of the economics ministry, told the state-run Central News Agency.
Taiwan has suspended all aid projects and treaties in protest against the decision to break diplomatic ties.
Cho was quoted as saying he would not be surprised to see many Taiwan-funded firms -- especially money-losing textile companies -- terminate their operations in South Africa soon.
